**Code and data:** all analysis for this report is reproducible from the repository at <https://github.com/USER/REPO>. <!-- See rubric: Code repository -->

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

# Load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(modelsummary)
library(knitr)

data <- read_csv("data/final_model_data.csv") |>
  mutate(year = factor(year), mode = factor(mode, levels = c(
    "Phone", "Internet",
    "Mixed / Other"
  )))

# Regression models that explore how polling characteristics are associated
# to error
model_1 <- lm(abs_error ~ days_prior, data = data)
model_2 <- lm(abs_error ~ days_prior + year, data = data)
model_3 <- lm(abs_error ~ days_prior + year + sample_size_log, data = data)
model_4 <- lm(abs_error ~ days_prior + year + sample_size_log + mode,
  data = data
)

# Pull values out so they can be reported inline (never hard-type a number)
timing_beta <- coef(model_1)[["days_prior"]]
r2_m1 <- summary(model_1)$r.squared

year_beta <- coef(model_2)[["year2016"]]
r2_m2 <- summary(model_2)$r.squared

size_beta <- coef(model_3)[["sample_size_log"]]
r2_m3 <- summary(model_3)$r.squared

internet_beta <- coef(model_4)[["modeInternet"]]
mixed_beta <- coef(model_4)[["modeMixed / Other"]]
r2_m4 <- summary(model_4)$r.squared

n_obs <- nrow(data)
```

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Election polls have a vital role in examining voter preferences and influencing expectations about electoral results. However, their stated precision does not automatically guarantee accuracy. In the Journal of the American Statistical Association, @shiranimehr2018 discovered that observed polling errors were around double the implied conventional margins of error, emphasising that polling uncertainty extends beyond random sampling variability. This prompts a question about whether polling characteristics can explain differences in the accuracy of polls.

The 2012 and 2016 US presidential elections offer a valuable basis for exploring this question. Particularly, state-level polling in the election year 2016 demonstrated substantial errors, with @kennedy2018 noting a mean absolute error of 5.1 percentage points. The journal article states that late swings in voter preferences and insufficient adjustments for educational attainment were key factors that led to such errors.

These findings further motivate an examination into whether polling timing, sample size, and survey methodology are associated with the accuracy of polling results. Hence, this report investigates the research question: **To what degree are polling timing, sample size and methodology associated with the accuracy of state-level presidential polls for the 2012 and 2016 elections.** More specifically, it explores:

1\. Whether polling accuracy is associated with days prior to Election Day

2\. Whether election year, sample size and methodology explain variation in polling errors once timing is accounted for

Polling accuracy is measured as the absolute error between polling and actual Democratic-Republican voting margins. Multiple linear regression models are utilised as a means to explore these relationships.

# Method {#sec-method}

## Data

This report utilises state-level presidential polling data from the US election years 2012 and 2016. This data was retrieved from HuffPost Pollster via the pollstR R package on 10 January 2017 as part of the rOpenGov project. Official election results were obtained from the MIT Election Data and Science Lab’s US President 1976-2024 dataset, accessed via the Harvard Dataverse. Following the data preparation, the unit of observation in the final dataset is an individual state-level poll, which can be identified using election year, state and poll ID.

Initial data cleaning and standardisation was completed previously in the Exploratory Data Analysis Report. These datasets can be found in the data folder within the GitHub Repository (add in link). For the following analysis, party candidate support percentages for Democratic and Republican were combined into a single observation per poll. Polling margins were measured as the difference between Republican and Democratic support (Democratic – Republican). A similar calculation was used for actual election outcomes, with electoral margins being measured using each party’s share of total state votes. Polls were matched to election observations based on state and year.

The response variable, absolute polling error, calculates the absolute difference between polling and election margins in terms of percentage points. Explanatory variables to be used include:

-   days_prior: the number of days between poll’s end date and the relevant Election Day

-   sample_size_log: the logarithm of the sample size for the poll

-   mode: polling methodology (Phone, Internet and Mixed/Other)

-   year: election year – either 2012 or 2016

As noted, sample size was logarithmically transformed given there may be a potentially nonlinear relationship with polling error. Additionally, the mode variable was consolidated from 8 categories into 3 groups: Phone, Internet and Mixed/Other. This consolidated reduced the number of different categories with minimal observations, enabling a more effective comparison between polling modes.

Any observations that were incomplete or had invalid values for the variables required for regression modelling were excluded, enabling consistent samples across all models. The final dataset consists of `r n_obs` observations. The descriptive statistics for this dataset is displayed in @tbl-descriptives. The additional data cleaning and preparation is fully documented in @sec-appendix.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-descriptives
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive statistics of numerical variables"

data |>
  summarise(
    across(c(abs_error, days_prior, sample_size),
      list(mean = mean, sd = sd, median = median),
      .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(),
    names_to = c("Variable", ".value"),
    names_sep = "_(?=[^_]+$)"
  ) |>
  kable(digits = 2, col.names = c("Variable", "Mean", "SD", "Median"))

data |>
  count(year, mode) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(percent = 100 * n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  kable(digits = 1, col.names = c(
    "Election year", "Mode",
    "No. of polls", "Percent (%)"
  ))
```

## Statistical methods

Multiple linear regressions using ordinary least squares was utilised to explore associations between polling characteristics and absolute polling error. The use of this method allowed for the relationship between polling timing and error to be examined, while accounting for other explanatory variables.

A total of four nested regression models were constructed to address the central research question. Model 1 investigates the association between polling time and absolute error. Model 2 includes an additional explanatory variable for year to account for differences between 2012 and 2016 elections. Model 3 adds log-transformed sample size, and Model 4 further includes polling mode to investigate methodological differences once adjusting for other variables. This final model considers absolute polling error as a function of timing, election year, sample size and mode.

In these models, election year and polling mode were treated as categorical variables, with 2012 and Phone as the respective reference categories. The coefficients of the models were interpreted as changes in expected absolute polling error (in percentage points), accounting for other predictors included in the given model.

Model assumptions including linearity, constant variance, and residual normality were assessed through residual versus fitted and normal Q-Q plots. Additionally, influential observations were also investigated using standard regression diagnostics. Potential dependence between polls from the same state or pollster was considered a possible limitation of the assumption of independence. Given that absolute errors are non-negative and possibly right-skewed, assumption checking is especially relevant. The analysis remains observational, meaning any relationships should not be considered as causal. Detailed model specifications, diagnostics, and R code is fully documented and can be found in @sec-appendix.

# Results {#sec-results}

As displayed in @fig-timing, absolute polling error tends to increase with greater number of days remaining before Election Day. This suggests that polls carried out earlier appear to deviate more from the actual election results. The 2016 polls also indicate greater errors compared to 2012, but there is moderate variation for both election years. These preliminary relationships are further investigated in a formal manner using multiple linear regression, with estimated models showcased in @tbl-model.

```{r}
#| label: fig-timing
#| fig-cap: "Absolute polling error in Democratic-Republican vote margins (pp)
#| against number of days the poll was conducted prior to the 2012 and 2016
#| elections. Each point indicates an individual poll, with grey representing
#| election year 2012, and navy indicating 2016. Solid lines are fitted linear
#| trends using OLS for each election year, and shaded bands represent 95%
#| confidence interval. Figure suggests that polls conducted further from the
#| election date tend to have larger errors, while errors are mostly greater in
#| 2016. The model doesn't account for sample size and polling mode, and
#| larger errors could possibly indicate changes in voter preferences nearing
#| election day."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(data, aes(x = days_prior, y = abs_error, colour = year)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 4, alpha = 0.2, size = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("2012" = "#4D4D4D", "2016" = "#21618C")) +
  labs(
    x = "Days prior to election", y = "Absolute polling error (pp)",
    colour = "Election Year"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-model
#| tbl-cap: "Multiple linear regression exploring association between polling
#| characteristics and absolute polling error for 2012 and 2016 US
#| presidential elections."
# modelsummary's default `tinytable` backend renders cleanly to PDF.

modelsummary(
  list(
    "Model 1" = model_1, "Model 2" = model_2, "Model 3" = model_3,
    "Model 4" = model_4
  ),
  coef_map = c(
    "(Intercept)" = "Intercept",
    "days_prior" = "Days before Election",
    "year2016" = "2016 election (vs 2012)",
    "sample_size_log" = "Log sample size",
    "modeInternet" = "Internet (vs Phone)",
    "modeMixed / Other" = "Mixed/Other (vs Phone)"
  ),
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared", "adj.r.squared"),
  stars = TRUE
)
```

The regression estimates displayed in @tbl-model offer further evidence of an association between polling timing and absolute polling error. In Model 1, each additional day before the elections is associated with a `r round(timing_beta, 3)` percentage point (`r round(timing_beta, 3)`%) increase in absolute error. Over 100 days, this corresponds to an increase of around `r round(100*timing_beta, 3)` percentage points. Across all four models, the relationship between poll timing and error remains positive and statistically significant, after accounting for sample size, mode and election year. This pattern indicates that polling timing is consistently associated with accuracy. In saying this, the magnitude of the relationship is modest.

Model 2 introduces the election year, and substantially improves explanatory power. This can be seen from the R squared value increasing from `r round(r2_m1, 3)` to `r round(r2_m2, 3)`. This means that including election year increases the amount of variation that can be explained by the model by approximately `r round(100*(r2_m2 - r2_m1), 3)` percentage points. The estimated coefficient for 2016 is positive and statistically significant (p \< 0.001) for models including the predictor. Specifically, the coefficient of `r round(year_beta, 3)` suggests that polls from the 2016 election had approximately `r round(year_beta, 3)` percentage points greater absolute error than polls from the 2012 election, holding timing constant. The estimated coefficient changes throughout the models, but remains statistically significant even after accounting for sample size and polling model in Model 4. These findings suggest that difference between election years is able to explain more variation in polling error than timing alone.

Models 3 and 4 extend the model by adding sample size and polling mode respectively. The estimated coefficient for log sample size is `r round(size_beta, 3)`, meaning that doubling the number of respondents is associated with approximately `r round(abs(log(2) * size_beta), 3)` percentage points lower absolute error when holding all other predictors constant. On the other hand, polling mode offers minimal additional explanatory value. Relative to polls conducted via phone (reference category), internet polls tend to have approximately `r round(internet_beta, 3)` percentage points greater error, while Mixed/Other polls have `r round(abs(mixed_beta), 3)` percentage points less error. However, neither coefficients appear to be statistically significant at the 5% level, meaning there is not enough evidence of difference in error between the different polling modes and Phone polls after adjusting for other predictors.

Overall, polling timing, election year, and sample size indicated statistically significant associations with absolute polling error, while polling model did not. While there was improvements from the initial model (Model 1), the final model (Model 4) only explained `r round(100*(r2_m4), 3)`% of the variation in the data, suggesting that majority of the variation remains unexplained by the 4 predictors. Regression diagnostic and assumption checks can be found in @sec-appendix.


Discussion:
This report investigated whether a range of polling characteristics were associated with absolute polling error in the 2012 and 2016 US presidential elections. Overall, the results highlighted that timing, election year, and sample size are statistically significant predictors of absolute error, while methodology has minimal additional explanatory value. However, it is important to note that the final model explains only a modest proportion of variation in the polling error, indicating the limitations of these characteristics. 

The first research question posed an investigation into the relationship between polling timing and error. The findings showed that polls conducted further from Election Day were associated with larger absolute error. This positive relationship was present after adjusting for other polling factors, meaning that timing contributed independently to explaining some variation in polling accuracy. However, this finding does not provide evidence that earlier polls were conducted inaccurately. Voter preferences may shift from the date of polling to Election Day, so earlier polls could have accurately represented public opinion at the time while differing from final election results. Therefore, the outcome measure involves both polling error and changes in voting preferences, a fundamental distinction when interpreting the results.   

The second research question indicated that election year was the strongest characteristic in improving explanatory power of the model. Adding election year increases the R squared value from `r round(r2_m1, 3)` to `r round(r2_m2, 3)`, suggesting that differences between the two election years explains more variation than timing solely. The positive coefficient suggests greater absolute errors in 2016, which is consistent with the American Association for Public Opinion Research's examination of the 2016 election, where @kennedy2018's findings suggest late changes in voter preferences and inadequate weighting for educational attainment as factors contributing to the state-level polling errors. Given those factors were not measured in the analysis, they remain potential explanations, not found causes of the observed election year difference.

Increases in sample sizes were also associated with smaller polling errors, consistent with the expectation that a greater number of respondents will reduce random sampling variability. However, the minimal increase in the R-squared value after implementing sample size into the model indicates that additional explanatory value is limited. Furthermore, sample size alone cannot ensure accuracy if systematic errors such as unrepresentative samples, non response or inappropriate weighting continue to persist. Polling mode was found to be not statistically significant once other predictors were accounted for. This does not necessarily mean that all polling methodologies are equally accurate as the general categories used in the final regression model may hide differences in the poll design and implementation. 

There are several limitations to be considered when analysing the results. Most evidently, the final model explains only `r round(100*(r2_m4), 3)`% of variation in polling error, meaning that a large proportion of variation remains unexplained from the model. Additionally, there are potentially relevant factors such as demographic weighting, likely-voter models and  state-level political conditions that were not accounted for in the models. Furthermore, observations from the same states could be correlated, potentially violating the assumption of independence. Diagnostic checks conducted in @sec-app-checks suggested possible heteroskedasticity, non-normal residuals and few influential observations, meaning there needs to be cautious interpretation of results. The observational nature of the study further prevents causal interpretations of the estimated relationships while the fact that the analysis focuses on two election years limits generalisability. 

Overall, the results suggest that election year and polling timing are able to better explain polling error than the broad methodology categories investigated. However, the limited explanatory power of the final model indicates these characteristics alone cannot sufficiently explain differences in polling error. Future studies around polling error and improving electoral forecasting should therefore take into account additional factors such as demographic representativeness, voter turnout and shifts in public opinion.

# Statistical appendix {#sec-appendix}

This appendix documents the analysis so the results above are fully reproducible.
The annotated code reproduces the model and its assumption checks; the complete
project (data, scripts, and commit history) is in the repository linked at the
top.

## Data preparation {#sec-app-data}

```{r}
#| label: appendix-data-preparation
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(readr)
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)

# Read cleaned datasets from EDA report
elections <- read_csv("data/1976-2024-president-clean.csv")
polls_2012 <- read_csv("data/state_polls_2012_clean.csv")
polls_2016 <- read_csv("data/state_polls_2016_clean.csv")


# Prepare 2012 polling data
# Convert observations into one row per poll
polls_2012_wide <- polls_2012 |>
  filter(candidate %in% c("Obama", "Romney")) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = candidate, values_from = support) |>
  # New column with election year
  mutate(year = 2012) |>
  # New column with poll margin (Dem - Rep)
  mutate(margin_poll = Obama - Romney)

# Prepare 2016 polling data
# Convert observations into one row per poll
polls_2016_wide <- polls_2016 |>
  filter(candidate %in% c("Clinton", "Trump")) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = candidate, values_from = support) |>
  # New column with election year
  mutate(year = 2016) |>
  # New column with poll margin (Dem - Rep)
  mutate(margin_poll = Clinton - Trump)

# Combine both election year polling data
polls_2012_2016 <- bind_rows(polls_2012_wide, polls_2016_wide) |>
  # Keep columns necessary for modelling
  select(year, state, poll_id, pollster, end_date, start_date, mode, sample_size, margin_poll)

# Check number of polls for each year after combining datasets
polls_2012_2016 |>
  count(year)

# Prepare election results
# Keep election results for only 2012 and 2016, Dem and Rep parties
margin_elections <- elections |>
  filter(year %in% c(2012, 2016)) |>
  # Sum votes across all Rep candidate records and then across all Dem candidate records
  group_by(year, state) |>
  summarise(
    votes_rep = sum(candidatevotes[party_simplified == "REPUBLICAN"],
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    votes_dem = sum(candidatevotes[party_simplified == "DEMOCRAT"],
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    # Count total votes in each state for each election year
    votes_total = first(totalvotes),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  # Calculate election Dem-Rep vote margin as percentage points
  mutate(margin_actual = 100 * (votes_dem - votes_rep) / votes_total)

# Create one dataset containing poll and election results
# Join polling votes with election outcomes
polls_and_elections <- polls_2012_2016 |>
  left_join(margin_elections |> select(year, state, margin_actual),
    by = c("year", "state")
  )
# Check if any polls had no matching election results
sum(is.na(polls_and_elections$margin_actual))

# Prepare regression variables for models
model_data <- polls_and_elections |>
  # Convert polling start and end dates into Date format
  mutate(
    start_date = as.Date(start_date),
    end_date = as.Date(end_date)
  ) |>
  # Add column for election date for the corresponding year
  mutate(election_date = as.Date(if_else(year == 2016, "2016-11-08", "2012-11-06"))) |>
  # Create column with number of days between poll and election
  mutate(days_prior = as.numeric(as.numeric(election_date - end_date))) |>
  # Create column with absolute polling error
  mutate(abs_error = abs(margin_poll - margin_actual)) |>
  # Create column to calculate logarithm of sample size
  mutate(sample_size_log = if_else(sample_size > 0 & !is.na(sample_size),
    log(sample_size),
    NA_real_
  )) |>
  # Election year to be treated as a cateogorical variable for modelling purposes
  mutate(year = factor(year)) |>
  # Polling mode to be condensed into 3 categories and be treated as categorical variable
  mutate(
    mode = case_when(
      mode %in% c(
        "Automated Phone", "Live Phone",
        "IVR/Live Phone"
      ) ~ "Phone",
      mode == "Internet" ~ "Internet",
      TRUE ~ "Mixed / Other"
    ),
    mode = factor(mode, levels = c("Phone", "Internet", "Mixed / Other"))
  )

# Check model dataset
# Check: all polls have distinct state-year-poll ID
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(model_data[c("year", "state", "poll_id")]))
# Check: all polls occur before Election day
stopifnot(all(model_data$days_prior >= 0, na.rm = TRUE))
# Check: missing values in variables
model_data |>
  summarise(
    error_miss = sum(is.na(abs_error)),
    year_miss = sum(is.na(year)),
    mode_miss = sum(is.na(mode)),
    sample_miss = sum(is.na(sample_size_log)),
    days_miss = sum(is.na(days_prior))
  )
# Understand distribution of polling modes
model_data |>
  count(year, mode)

# Construct final dataset for models
# Keep observations with no missing values (remove observations with missing sample size)
final_model_data <- model_data |>
  filter(!is.na(sample_size_log))
# Check final number of polls for each year
final_model_data |>
  count(year)
# Glimpse of final model dataset
glimpse(final_model_data)
# Summary of means for main numerical variables
final_model_data |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    err_mean = mean(abs_error),
    err_median = median(abs_error),
    days_mean = mean(days_prior),
    sample_mean = mean(sample_size)
  )

# Save dataset for regressional analysis in data folder
write_csv(final_model_data, "data/final_model_data.csv")
```

## Model {#sec-app-model}

Four OLS regression models were fitted to explore the association between polling characteristics and absolute polling error. The models progressively included timing, election year, log sample size and polling methodology. The comparison of these estimates can be found in @tbl-model. @tbl-model-detail reports the full fitted Model 4 with 95% confidence intervals.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-model-detail
#| tbl-cap: "Detailed OLS estimates for Model 4, exploring absolute polling error in 2012 and 2016 elections. Full regression results with 95% confidence intervals for all coefficients. Reference categories is 2012 (election year) and Phone (polling mode)."
#| echo: true
# Report fully adjusted model with 95% CI 

modelsummary(
  list("Model 4" = model_4),
  statistic = "conf.int",   # 95% CIs beneath each estimate
  coef_map  = c(
    "(Intercept)" = "Intercept",
    "days_prior" = "Days before Election",
    "year2016" = "2016 election (vs 2012)",
    "sample_size_log" = "Log sample size",
    "modeInternet" = "Internet (vs Phone)",
    "modeMixed / Other" = "Mixed/Other (vs Phone)"
  ),
  gof_map   = c("nobs", "r.squared", "adj.r.squared")
)
```

## Assumption checks {#sec-app-checks}

Regression diagnostics were carried out for Model 4 to check the aassumptions of linearity, equal variance and approximate normality of residuals. @fig-diagnostics displays residual against fitted values and the normal Q-Q plot for Model 4. An additional plot inspects any potentially influential observations using a Cook's distance plot. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-diagnostics
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Model 4 diagnostic checks: residual vs fitted values, normal Q-Q plot, and Cook's distance, examining assumptions of the model and any influential observations"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 10

# Display 3 plots vertically 
par(mfrow = c(3,1), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
# Residual vs fitted plot: checking linearity and equal variance
plot(model_4, which = 1)   

# Normal Q-Q plot: check normality of residuals 
plot(model_4, which = 2)

# Check potentially influential observations 
plot(model_4, which = 4)
```

The diagnostic plots in @fig-diagnostics showcases some deviations from the assumptions of OLS regression. The residual-vs-fitted plot presents a moderately flat smooth trend, but changes in dispersion may indicate heteroskedasticity. Because of this, standard errors and results may become somewhat unreliable. The normal Q-Q plot also showcases substantial deviation from the reference line, especially in the upper tail, suggesting positively-skewed, non-normal residuals. This is unsurprising as the dependent variable is absolute, which is bounded by 0 but can take large positive values. The Cook's distance plot notes a few potentially influential observations, most evidently observation 1289. These results mean that OLS standard errors and significance tests must be interpreted carefully.
